name: Carl Schmitt
summary: Carl Schmitt distinguished politics by the ability of a community to identify its public enemies and treated decisions in emergencies as a test of sovereignty. He criticized parliamentary liberalism and defended Nazi leadership and anti-Jewish exclusion in the 1930s. His postwar work interpreted international law through territorial orders and criticized attempts to enforce a universal political order.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Schmitt treated the organized capacity to fight and make war as essential to maintaining a political community against external enemies.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: In the chapter on changes of territory Schmitt treated effective conquest as capable of changing territorial sovereignty under the European interstate legal order without a vote of the inhabitants.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: In the section on the legal position of the partisan Schmitt treated organized resistance against a foreign occupier as capable of legitimate combatant status and distinguished local defense from war aimed at destroying an ideological enemy.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: In the discussion of legality and equal chance, Schmitt argued that equal access to power presupposed a willingness to preserve that opportunity for opponents and criticized allowing parties to exploit the rules to terminate constitutional legality.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: In the chapter on land, sea and air war Schmitt defended the European interstate model of limited warfare, under which opposing armies were the belligerents and the civilian population was protected.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Schmitt treated Marx’s analysis of class conflict as a diagnosis of industrialization in nineteenth-century Europe and rejected its extension into a general historical law.

conscription.rationale: In his Düsseldorf address Schmitt called universal military service the necessary counterpart of universal suffrage and rejected the exclusion of compulsory service from a democratic state.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In his discussion of the special threshold for constitutional amendment, Schmitt held that electoral and legislative majorities could not use ordinary lawmaking authority to overturn fundamental constitutional decisions.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Schmitt grounded democracy in the political identity of rulers and ruled and treated electoral procedures as dispensable when public acclamation expressed that identity.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Schmitt praised the 1935 law protecting German blood and honor, which prohibited marriages and sexual relations between Jews and people of German or related ancestry.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Schmitt warned that ethnic and other divisions could disintegrate a political community unless a strong state imposed unity, and made substantive homogeneity a condition of democracy.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In the opening chapter of Political Theology Schmitt grounded suspension of the law in the state’s right of self-preservation. He later applied that view to Hitler’s summary use of lethal force against perceived internal enemies in 1934.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Schmitt rejected equal legal treatment across groups that the Nazi state defined by ancestry and praised the Reich Citizenship Law for embedding that distinction in German public law.

ethnic-nation.rationale: In the section on leadership and ethnic identity, Schmitt made ethnic sameness between leaders and followers a condition of German political unity and praised the Nuremberg Laws for grounding public law in German ancestry.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Schmitt defended nonintervention between large political spaces and criticized the extension of regional doctrines into universal claims to intervene.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Schmitt praised the new constitutional order for uniting the position of head of state and supreme command of the armed forces in Hitler.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: In the section on plebiscitary legitimacy Schmitt treated the president’s dissolution of the Reichstag as a constitutional instrument for appealing to the people and criticized dissolutions that failed to present a clear question.

independent-unions.rationale: In the section on the Weimar constitution and liberal pluralism Schmitt criticized the autonomy of unions as private organizations. His proposed order placed trade associations within an economy subject to the political leadership of the Nazi movement.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: Schmitt argued that states invoking humanity to justify war turn a political adversary into an outlaw and use universal claims to license intervention and harsher warfare.

more-religion-public.rationale: In his discussion of representation Schmitt defended the Catholic Church’s public political form and described the Church and state as distinct institutions that should relate to each other as partners.

multipolar-world.rationale: Schmitt described political order as a plurality of independent entities and called for an international spatial order that could accommodate more than one great power.

national-rebirth.rationale: Schmitt presented the replacement of Weimar liberalism by the new racial and party order as a recovery of German political unity after centuries of constitutional disunity.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Schmitt held that an organized people may fight and physically kill those who threaten its collective form of existence.

night-watchman-state.rationale: In the fourth section of his Düsseldorf address Schmitt assigned the state exclusive responsibility for managing transport and broadcasting, alongside its functions of security and defense.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Schmitt’s theory of constitutional guardianship entrusted the Reich president with representing the political unity of the whole people against the sectional interests of the parties.

one-party-rule.rationale: In the section on his tripartite model of state, movement and people, Schmitt vested political leadership in the sole Nazi party and treated that movement as the guardian of the new constitution.

open-borders.rationale: In the preface to the second edition Schmitt defended the ability of a democracy to exclude would-be settlers through its immigration laws to preserve national homogeneity.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Schmitt argued that parliament had lost its justification as a body for open deliberation and accepted that direct or dictatorial forms could express the people’s political will.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: In his discussion of a second chamber Schmitt insisted that unanimity among organized economic interests breaks down in serious conflicts and that a political decision still has to be made.

political-violence-legitimate.rationale: In his account of the partisan’s legal status Schmitt recognized legitimacy for irregular armed resistance defending its homeland against an occupier.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Schmitt separated political enmity from moral evil and argued that a public enemy need have no moral defect.

population-transfer.rationale: Schmitt treated the expulsion of Greeks from Turkey as an example of enforcing national homogeneity and included expulsion among the measures a state could use in declaring an internal enemy.

private-courts-defense.rationale: In the description of his tripartite model Schmitt placed the administration of justice within the state. He vested ultimate judicial authority in the political leader in emergencies.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: In his defense of the 1934 purge, Schmitt held that Hitler could create law directly as supreme judge when danger arose, without relying on the regular courts.

public-ownership.rationale: In the fourth section of his Düsseldorf address Schmitt reserved transport and broadcasting for the state while assigning other activity to economic self-administration or free enterprise.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: In the preface to the second edition Schmitt cited Australia’s racially exclusionary immigration policy as an example of using border controls to preserve national homogeneity.

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: In the chapter on changes of territory Schmitt treated effective conquest as a recognized basis of sovereign title under the European interstate legal order and distinguished it from mere temporary occupation.

regulate-corporations.rationale: In the Düsseldorf address Schmitt called for the state to disentangle itself from economic management by leaving a large sphere to free enterprise and a separate sphere to self-administering economic bodies.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Schmitt’s constitutional theory allows the constituent people to remake the political order by an act of sovereign dictatorship outside the amendment procedures of the existing constitution.

separate-church-state.rationale: In his discussion of representation Schmitt envisaged a partnership between the Catholic Church and the political state, both with publicly representative roles.

separated-powers.rationale: Schmitt treated supreme judicial power as vested in the political leader in an emergency and applied the same leadership principle across public institutions.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Schmitt held that in the emergency Hitler could make a supreme judicial decision directly and that ordinary judicial authorities could not review that act.

state-class-instrument.rationale: In section 4 Schmitt rejected the pluralist account that makes the state a servant of an economically determined society and insisted that a state capable of political decision has authority independent of competing social groups.

state-harmful.rationale: Schmitt assigned the state the task of securing domestic order and the authority to decide on enemies so the political community could defend its existence.

strong-leader.rationale: Schmitt placed the leadership principle throughout public institutions and argued that Hitler could exercise supreme judicial authority by direct decision in a crisis.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: In his discussion of representation Schmitt understood the Church as a public institution capable of entering into partnership with the state on the strength of its own independent authority.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Schmitt justified the 1934 purge as an act of supreme justice and held that a state may designate domestic enemies when its existence is at stake.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: In The Age of Neutralizations and Depoliticizations, Schmitt rejected the expectation that technological progress would bring moral or political reconciliation and argued that competing groups can use the same technologies against one another.

total-state.rationale: In the Düsseldorf address and his tripartite model of state, movement and people, Schmitt assigned economic and communal life a sphere of self-administration. He insisted that political leadership set its limits.

unions-run-economy.rationale: In the Düsseldorf address and his tripartite model of state, movement and people, Schmitt allowed trade associations a role in self-administration while assigning other sectors to the state and free enterprise.

notes: Reviewed constitutional design, parties, elections, emergency law, civil liberties, anti-Jewish legal exclusion and cultural policy, church–state relations, private economic organization, wartime rules, territorial changes, nonintervention, international organization, technology, and ecology. Schmitt’s 1933–35 writings defend Nazi institutions, while his later international-law writings address relations among political orders. The organization of the 1936 conference is documented, but it does not by itself establish a general policy on the quiz’s separate speech, media, and education questions. The Düsseldorf address and the writings on economic self-administration, industrialization, and class conflict were checked again after the first uncertainty calculation. The record contains much more on the institutional division between the state and economic actors than on tax, welfare, or labor-market instruments.
